subject: English
topic: Phrase Replacement / Sentence Improvement — SSC CGL Favourite Pattern (W13 B1)

questions.stem: Identify the correct replacement for the underlined part, or choose 'No improvement': 'She is _good_ in singing but weak in dancing.' (underlined: good)
questions.explanation: A is correct. The correct preposition with 'good' when referring to skill is 'AT'. 'Good AT singing' — not 'good in'. Similarly: good at mathematics, good at playing guitar. 'Good in' is non-standard in this context (it is used informally in some Indian English but is incorrect in standard grammar). The parallel with 'weak in' is a trap — both should ideally use 'at', but the question targets replacing 'good in' only. SSC PYQ pattern: preposition after 'good' = AT (skill/activity).

questions.stem: Identify the correct replacement or 'No improvement': 'He is used to _work_ late into the night.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Used to + verb' (meaning habitual past action) takes a BASE FORM. 'Is used to + gerund' (meaning accustomed to) takes a GERUND. 'He is used to working late' = he is accustomed to it (present habit). 'To' here is a PREPOSITION, not a to-infinitive marker. After prepositions, always use V+ing. Trap: 'work' (base form) = correct after 'used to' meaning past habit ('he used to work late'), but wrong after 'is used to'; 'No improvement' = wrong because 'work' in original is the error.

questions.stem: Identify the correct replacement or 'No improvement': 'The team, along with their manager, _are_ travelling to Mumbai.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. When a phrase like 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with', 'in addition to' connects subjects, the verb agrees with the FIRST subject only (not the phrase in between). 'The team' (singular) + 'along with their manager' → verb = IS. 'Are' is wrong. Correct: 'The team, along with their manager, IS travelling.' SSC repeats this rule constantly. Compare: 'The manager, along with the team, IS travelling' — same rule applies. Trap: 'were' = past tense (wrong — sentence is present).

questions.stem: Identify the correct replacement or 'No improvement': 'No sooner did she enter the room _then_ the lights went out.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. The idiom is 'no sooner...THAN' (not 'then' or 'when'). 'No sooner did she enter THAN the lights went out.' Compare: 'scarcely/hardly/barely...WHEN/BEFORE'. The distinction: 'no sooner' pairs with 'than'; 'scarcely/hardly' pairs with 'when' or 'before'. Trap: 'when' = used with scarcely/hardly/barely (not with no sooner); 'then' = the most common error (students confuse then/than in comparisons); 'as' = used in 'as soon as' construction (different structure).

questions.stem: Identify the correct replacement or 'No improvement': 'The police is investigating the case of missing funds.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Police' is always treated as a PLURAL noun in standard English (unlike 'police force' which can be singular). 'The police ARE investigating' — even though 'police' looks singular, it refers to multiple officers. Other always-plural nouns: people, cattle, public, gentry, clergy. Trap: 'was investigating' = singular past (doubly wrong — wrong number AND wrong tense from context); 'No improvement' = 'police is' in the original is the error.

questions.stem: Identify the correct replacement or 'No improvement': 'He prevented me to attend the meeting.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Prevent' takes the pattern: prevent + object + FROM + gerund. 'Prevented me FROM attending.' Not 'to attend' (infinitive). SSC favourite: stop/prevent/prohibit/restrain + object + FROM + V-ing. Also: 'He stopped me from leaving.' Trap: 'prevented me attending' = missing the obligatory 'from' (acceptable in very informal speech but wrong in formal grammar); 'for attending' = wrong preposition.

questions.stem: Identify the correct replacement or 'No improvement': 'The number of road accidents have increased sharply this year.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'THE number of + plural noun' = singular subject → singular verb. 'The number of road accidents HAS increased.' Contrast: 'A number of road accidents HAVE occurred' (a number of = many = plural). The/A distinction is a top SSC repeat: 'A number of' = many (plural verb); 'The number of' = the count (singular verb). Trap: 'are increasing' = continuous (wrong aspect — 'sharply this year' suggests completed change, better with perfect); 'had increased' = past perfect (implies an earlier-still-relevant past action, wrong with 'this year').

questions.stem: Identify the correct replacement or 'No improvement': 'I look forward to hear from you soon.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Look forward TO' — the 'to' is a PREPOSITION here (not the infinitive marker). After prepositions, use GERUND (V+ing). 'Look forward TO HEARING from you.' This is the classic SSC/business-letter trap. Other 'to + gerund' expressions: object to (V+ing), used to (V+ing), addicted to (V+ing), in addition to (V+ing), devoted to (V+ing). Trap: 'to hear' = treats 'to' as infinitive marker (wrong); 'for hearing' = wrong preposition entirely.

questions.stem: Identify the correct replacement or 'No improvement': 'One of my friends have gone abroad.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'ONE of my friends' — the subject is 'ONE' (singular), not 'friends' (plural). Verb agrees with 'one' → singular → HAS gone. 'Have gone' is wrong. Pattern: 'One of the + plural noun + SINGULAR verb.' Also correct: 'Each of them IS going'; 'Neither of the two WAS present.' Trap: 'are gone' = treats 'friends' as the subject (wrong — subject is 'one'); 'had went' = wrong past participle (should be 'had gone'); 'No improvement' = original 'have gone' is the error.

questions.stem: Identify the correct replacement or 'No improvement': 'Hardly had the match begun when it started to rain heavily.'
questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Hardly had + subject + Past Participle + when...' is the CORRECT structure. 'Hardly had the match BEGUN when it started to rain' is grammatically perfect. Inversion after 'hardly/scarcely/no sooner' is mandatory, and 'begun' (past participle of begin) is correct. Trap: 'begin' = base form (wrong — must be past participle after 'had'); 'Hardly the match had begun' = no inversion (wrong — after 'hardly' at sentence start, inversion is required); 'Hardly had the match started' = 'started' is also a past participle and grammatically valid, making 'No improvement' more clearly the right choice here.
